*Grave of the Fireflies* was Takahata's first animated film produced with [Studio Ghibli](/wiki/Studio_Ghibli "Studio Ghibli").[[3]](#cite_note-:0-4)

Production of *Grave of the Fireflies* and *[My Neighbor Totoro](/wiki/My_Neighbor_Totoro "My Neighbor Totoro")* proceeded simultaneously at Ghibli. It is said that even [Toei Dōga](/wiki/Toei_Animation "Toei Animation") had never worked on two feature-length films at the same time, and since there were only a limited number of key staff members (animators) who could meet the high standards of Takahata and Miyazaki, the production team struggled to manage their personnel.[[32]](#cite_note-35) A particular point of contention was the treatment of animation director [Yoshifumi Kondō](/wiki/Yoshifumi_Kond%C5%8D "Yoshifumi Kondō"). As a result, while Miyazaki's team focused on newly recruited staff, Takahata's team gathered veteran staff members he had known for years, such as Kondō, [Yoshiyuki Momose](/wiki/Yoshiyuki_Momose "Yoshiyuki Momose") and art director Yamamoto.[[33]](#cite_note-36)[[34]](#cite_note-37)[[35]](#cite_note-38) In later recollections, Takahata stated that securing Kondō was his "top priority—no, an absolute must" in terms of personnel, and that he did not personally recruit any other members.[[36]](#cite_note-24nen-39)

The location and background in the film is based on a style created by 18th century Japanese artist [Hiroshige](/wiki/Hiroshige "Hiroshige") and his follower [Hergé](/wiki/Herg%C3%A9 "Hergé"), who created [Tintin](/wiki/Tintin_(character) "Tintin (character)").[[37]](#cite_note-:4-40) Film critic [Roger Ebert](/wiki/Roger_Ebert "Roger Ebert") examines the contrast of the style of the background in comparison to the cartoonish animation of the characters. Place names with *Neder*, *Nieder*, *Nedre*, *Nether*, *Lage(r)* or *Low(er)* (in [Germanic languages](/wiki/Germanic_languages "Germanic languages")) and *Bas* or *Inferior* (in [Romance languages](/wiki/Romance_languages "Romance languages")) are in use in low-lying places all over Europe. The original budget for construction of the stadium was $1.8 billion.[[76]](#cite_note-76) The budget was increased twice in 2019.[[77]](#cite_note-77) The first time was in May 2019 when the trusses had to be retrofitted.[[78]](#cite_note-78) Don Webb received an additional $40 million at the May 23, 2020, Stadium Authority Board meeting to cover the overages.[[79]](#cite_note-79) The second time was in September 2019. Don Webb received another $90 million to cover the extra shifts required to fix the broken truss issue.[[80]](#cite_note-80) The overages increased the new budget to $1.97 billion; $200 million over the original budget of $1.8 billion. Ultimately, the stadium was completed $25 million under the increased budget but $175 million over the original $1.8 billion budget.[[81]](#cite_note-81)

Of this $2 billion, $78 million was spent to purchase the land, $1.33 billion was spent on construction, $123 million on furniture, fixtures, and equipment, $234 million on design and engineering, and $31 million on utilities and infrastructure.[[82]](#cite_note-82)[[83]](#cite_note-83) Some reports gave a budget of $2 billion, which also included $100 million to build a separate Raiders practice facility.[[84]](#cite_note-84)

The financing for the project came in the form of $750 million in public funding and $1.1 billion from the Raiders.[[85]](#cite_note-85) The public portion of the funding came from [municipal bonds](/wiki/Municipal_bonds "Municipal bonds") issued by Clark County, backed by the proceeds of a [special tax on hotel rooms](/wiki/Hotel_tax "Hotel tax") in the Las Vegas area, which took effect in March 2017.[[86]](#cite_note-86) The Raiders' contribution included a $650 million loan from [Bank of America](/wiki/Bank_of_America "Bank of America"), $200 million from the NFL's stadium loan program, and $300 million from sales of [personal seat licenses](/wiki/Personal_seat_licenses "Personal seat licenses")

Leucine :: Synthesis in nonhuman organisms :: chunk_0006
Leucine is an essential amino acid in the diet of animals because they lack the complete enzyme pathway to synthesize it *de novo* from potential precursor compounds. Consequently, they must ingest it, usually as a component of proteins. Plants and microorganisms synthesize leucine from [pyruvic acid](/wiki/Pyruvic_acid "Pyruvic acid") with a series of enzymes:[[43]](#cite_note-44)

* [Acetolactate synthase](/wiki/Acetolactate_synthase "Acetolactate synthase")
* Acetohydroxy acid isomero[reductase](/wiki/Reductase "Reductase")
* [Dihydroxyacid dehydratase](/wiki/Dihydroxyacid_dehydratase "Dihydroxyacid dehydratase")
* [α-Isopropylmalate synthase](/wiki/%CE%91-Isopropylmalate_synthase "Α-Isopropylmalate synthase")
* [α-Isopropylmalate isomerase](/wiki/%CE%91-Isopropylmalate_isomerase "Α-Isopropylmalate isomerase")
* Leucine [aminotransferase](/wiki/Aminotransferase "Aminotransferase")

Synthesis of the small, hydrophobic amino acid [valine](/wiki/Valine "Valine") also includes the initial part of this pathway.

[![](//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/f/f8/Betain-Leucin.png/500px-Betain-Leucin.png)](/wiki/File:Betain-Leucin.png)

(*S*)-Leucine (or L-leucine), left; (*R*)-leucine (or D-leucine), right, in zwitterionic form at neutral pH

Leucine is a branched-chain amino acid (BCAA) since it possesses an [aliphatic](/wiki/Aliphatic "Aliphatic") side chain that is not linear.

[Racemic](/wiki/Racemic "Racemic") leucine had been subjected to circularly [polarized](/wiki/Polarization_(waves) "Polarization (waves)") [synchrotron radiation](/wiki/Synchrotron_radiation "Synchrotron radiation") to better understand the origin of biomolecular asymmetry.
